## 🏷️ Perfect matchings and relative approximation

A perfect matching of a finite undirected graph uses exactly one edge at each vertex. Write Z(G) for the number of perfect matchings. Finding one matching and counting all matchings are different tasks; sampling all matchings, regardless of size, does not automatically estimate the possibly tiny perfect-matching contribution.

A fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme, or FPRAS, returns Z satisfying

​Pr[(1−ε)Z≤Z≤(1+ε)Z]≥1−δ,​

in time polynomial in the input length, ε−1, and lo g(δ−1). This is a relative-error statement, so the zero-count case requires particular care.

> Counting manuscript statement
> 
> There is a uniform FPRAS for perfect matchings in every finite simple undirected graph. It returns zero on every execution when no perfect matching exists, and has a polynomial bit-time bound on every random tape, including unsuccessful ones. The stated parameter range is 0<ε<1 and 0<δ<1/2. (OpenAI, 2026)

The input need not be bipartite or dense. The second manuscript in the family studies entropy at prescribed matching marginals and a different, coarser deterministic approximation. Those estimates should not be confused with the FPRAS.

## 🏷️ Weighted laws and an annealing identity

Give each edge a positive activity w e​ and each perfect matching weight ∏e∈M​w e​. The partition function is the sum of these weights. Its normalized weights define a probability law.

The counting proof begins with a complete graph, whose perfect-matching count on 2 m vertices is (2 m−1)(2 m−3)⋯1, then gradually suppresses edges absent from G. For neighboring weight systems, the ratio of partition functions is an expectation under the earlier law:

Z(w)Z(w′)​=E w​e∈M∏​w e​w e′​​.

Multiplying estimated neighboring ratios recovers the final count from the known initial one. The proof must control accumulated error, residual weight from suppressed edges, and the cost of obtaining the samples.

Vertex scaling preserves the matching law. If w uv​ is multiplied by a u​a v​, every perfect matching gains exactly the common factor ∏v​a v​, because it meets every vertex once. This allows the source to balance local quantities without changing normalized probabilities. The required scales are learned from two-hole partition ratios, obtained by deleting pairs of vertices.
